chapter_theme: Poems of the fighting men and their households: the rites that guard a wounded man, the deaths of warriors from old martial houses, the mothers who weep and rejoice over sons, and the toddy, flowers and land a king owes those who go first.

281.reading: A woman calls her dear friend to come and guard the wound of the great man who took on the king's trouble: hang neem with iravam in the house, sound the lute and many instruments, smear the dark paste, scatter mustard, blow the ampal pipe, ring the bell, sing kaanchi and burn incense through the long house.
281.nuance: The whole poem is a list of household rites and only the last line says whose wound it is, so the wound is guarded as much by the women's noise and smoke as by medicine; ampal here is the pipe that is blown, not the water-lily.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed is guarding a wounded man's life with rites against harmful powers

282.reading: If you ask where the great doer is who paid his hard debt to the land with a spear through his chest, the answer is that holding the oncoming army he was cut down until neither body nor life could be seen, and nothing of him is left on the field but his split shield, yet he lives on, fame set far, in the mouths of poets.
282.nuance: The poem answers the question 'where is he?' twice: nowhere on the field, where even the body is gone, and in the poets' speech, so the poem itself is offered as the place where the hero now is.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's death holding back the oncoming army

283.reading: Through a broken text: after a scene of a cool pond where the vaalai fish and the otter take their daily prey and turn back from the crocodile, the poem names the unsubmitting Azhumbil man and the assembly of the Kosar, the women of soft shoulders playing with sand dolls, and a hero who wore the fragrant thumbai on his forehead.
283.nuance: Lines 7 and 12 are gaps and line 3 is read differently in another edition, so who the Azhumbil man is to the hero (enemy or lord) cannot be fixed; the Kosar, a people, are not one of the entity types and are noted here.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero wears the battle flower; the rest is too broken to decide on

284.reading: When the king's messengers cry everywhere 'let him come quickly', the man of an old fighting house comes alone on foot, garlanded, holds the hard battle, and while he straightens his bent sword against the tusk of the elephant he killed in front, he laughs at the back of the man who fled from him.
284.nuance: The elephant's tusk becomes a tool for mending the sword, so the kill is already work done; the laugh is the poem's last word and it is aimed at a back, the one part of a fighter that should not be seen.

thinai_evidence.note: a lone warrior holding a battle against an army

285.reading: Through a damaged text: in the camp the drummer holds the spear and the bard the shield; a warrior with a faded garland, his chest pierced by a long spear, fell to the ground with his fat-smeared anklet, all who saw it praised him, and his lord bowed his head, because to this leader of a poor kin he had given only a small village of barren land and not the cool fields where the grain-ears sway.
285.nuance: On this reading the lord's bow is shame, not grief: the man's death exposes how little he was paid, so the poem judges the giver; with lines 5 and 9 broken, whether it was the lord who gave the barren village is the likeliest but not a certain reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's event is a warrior's death in battle, which the lord's response follows

286.reading: Avvaiyar's speaker sets her son, who held out his bowl above many, against the other youths who remain like rams of white goats, and says it has not laid him on a bier with bound feet and covered him in pure white cloth.
286.nuance: The closing negative can be read as a plain statement (he died on the field and was not even carried home and shrouded) or as an exclamation (has it not laid him on the bier!); either way the son who was first to the king's bowl is set apart from the youths who survive.

thinai_evidence.note: the shroud and bier make the poem about a son's death

comparisons.tenor: the other youths, many and alike and unharmed

287.reading: Speaking to the drum-beating pulaiyan, the poet says that warriors of pride who do not run though arrows hit like the seasonal rain, spears flash like kendai fish in the paddy and an elephant drives its tusk into them, care nothing for winning cool fields where vaalai fish roll at the granary's foot, since if they die they enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the high world; so watch the upstart king's army come from here.
287.nuance: The poem names the two rewards of the hero side by side and ranks them: land if he lives is waved aside with யாவது, and the reward that counts is in the high world, which is a Sangam poem itself making heaven, not only fame, the warrior's wage.

thinai_evidence.note: a boast made as an invading army approaches

288.reading: The drum covered with the unshaved hide of the winner of two bulls set to fight sounds in the middle ground; in the confused battle a long spear pierced the warrior's heart that knew shame, and on his blood-swaying chest the kites crowded so thick they left no room for an embrace.
288.nuance: The drum's hide is itself the trophy of a fight between bulls, so the poem opens on one victor's skin and ends on another's body; who came to embrace him was in the lost line 7, and the kites have taken that place.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's death in the press of battle

289.reading: As a ploughman, even when the wet season has favoured him, looks among his many bulls for the best one, the king looks among the men of old fighting houses and says of the gold bowl raised for himself, 'give it to this one'; and more, hear, bard, the drummer in the camp crying 'today is the taking of flowers'.
289.nuance: The honour and the death are announced together: the bowl the king gives is the sign of who will go first, and the drum that follows calls the flower-taking for battle, so the chosen man is being picked as the ploughman picks the bull for the hardest furrow.

thinai_evidence.note: the drum announces the taking of the battle flowers before a fight

comparisons.tenor: the king choosing among the warriors

290.reading: Give this man toddy before you drink, lord of war elephants: his father's father stood unblinking and died, like the hub the carpenter fits the spokes into, beside your father's father in battle, and this man too, full of martial fame, will cover you from the spear aimed at you like thatch in the rain.
290.nuance: The claim to the first cup rests on a debt between two lines, not on this man's own deeds, and the two similes are both household things (the wheel hub, the roof thatch), so the warrior is made part of the king's house.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a warrior's inherited excellence, spoken to his king

comparisons.tenor: the grandfather standing as the spears were driven into him
this warrior shielding the king from spears

291.reading: The bard tells the children and drummers to keep the birds' clamour off the dark man lying under pure white cloth while she drives off the white jackal with the turning of a lament tune, and wishes on the king the same great trembling she feels, for he once put his own gem-like garland on the man who longed to die and wore the dead man's single-strand garland himself.
291.nuance: The exchange of garlands is the poem's charge against the king: by wearing the warrior's garland he took the warrior's place in a bond, so the mourner asks that he share the grief too; கொன்னும் makes the death look needless.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament sung over a dead warrior

292.reading: Do not be angry, petty men, that when the sweet cool toddy raised for the king was being mixed he stopped it and stood gripping his true sword: if he wants something, as he did here, he will not wait for his turn, and the manly one will stand there and stop the great army as it rises.
292.nuance: The speaker turns a breach of the feast's order into a promise: the same refusal to wait for his turn that offends at the toddy is what will hold the front, so his rudeness is offered as evidence of his courage.

thinai_evidence.note: the claim to the king's drink made at the feast before the army sets out

293.reading: If the summoning drum that the rider of the unflinching elephant beats against the hill-fort men sounds for men who know shame, the speaker asks, will the flower-selling woman, who has lost more of her beauty than we have, go into other people's houses as her trade: she is to be pitied.
293.nuance: The drum that sends men to take flowers for battle sends the flower-seller into houses that may soon be in mourning; who the 'we' are (the wives at home) and why she has lost more beauty than they is not said, so the pity may be for her poverty or for her trade in the flowers of the dead.

thinai_evidence.note: the war-drum's effect on those at home, seen through a poor woman

294.reading: In the sea-like camp under the moon of the white umbrella, in a battle so confused that kin cannot be told from foe, your husband called out his lord's name and his own, 'come here, you who would cut short our men's days', and stood fighting apart, and no one came near him, as no one comes near the gem a serpent has spat out.
294.nuance: Naming his lord and himself is the point: in a battle where nobody knows who is who, he makes himself known and so becomes untouchable, like the serpent's gem that is treasure and danger at once; குமரிப்படை in line 3 is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: a single warrior's stand in the press of battle

comparisons.tenor: the husband standing alone, whom no one approaches

295.reading: In the camp heaving like the sea, the young man of unretreating vow bit his lip, drove forward, split the oncoming army and lay broken apart in the middle of the press; seeing the glory of her excellent son, his mother's withered breasts welled and flowed.
295.nuance: The mother sees the body, not a report, and the response is in the body too: breasts long dry give milk again, as at his birth, so his death returns her to his infancy; the thurai's name holds joy and weeping together.

thinai_evidence.note: a son's death in battle and his mother's response

comparisons.tenor: the milk flowing from the mother's breasts

296.reading: Neem branches are broken, kaanchi is sung, mustard is smoked by ghee-smeared hands and every house is loud with it: is it that he fights on, burning with rage, that the great man's chariot is so long in coming?
296.nuance: The question in the last two lines is a hope disguised as a guess: the rites of 281 are already under way in every house, which suggests wounds, but the speaker reads the delay as rage still fighting.

thinai_evidence.note: the household rites that guard a fighter, with fear for his delay

297.reading: We do not want to seize this small village where the wild cow with her calf sleeps on a bed of threshed gram stalks whose pods are as long as a buffalo's horns; we want a grant, and blessing it with toddy from the jar it is right that cool fields by the ford where the waterhen lays her eggs be given to those who stand like the stiff-fronded palmyra, their chests pierced by the long spear.
297.nuance: The poem refuses plunder of a poor village and asks instead for a lawful grant, so it sets a limit on what the victors may take; the palmyra image gives the wounded men a standing posture even with spears in them.

thinai_evidence.note: the warriors' claim to the reward their wounds have earned

comparisons.tenor: the speared warriors who still stand

298.reading: The warrior complains of his king: he used to give us the dregs and drink the clear toddy himself, which was once his way; he is truly unkind, for now, besieging the enemy's strong fort, biting his lip and roaring, he does not say to me 'you go first'.
298.nuance: The grievance is not the poor drink but the denial of the vanguard: a warrior measures the king's favour by who is sent first to die, and மன் may mark the drinking order as a past custom now broken.

thinai_evidence.note: the setting is the siege of an enemy fort

299.reading: The horse of the chief of a small village fenced with cotton, slow-gaited from eating gram stalks, cleaved the battle-front like a boat driving into the sea, while the garlanded, ghee-fed, mane-clipped horses of the kings of rich fields held back, like women who may not touch the vessels in fearsome Murugan's shrine.
299.nuance: Every detail is set in pairs, cotton fence against cool fields, gram stalks against ghee, so the poem argues that feeding and finery do not make a warhorse; the second simile turns the rich horses' hanging back into a ritual bar rather than open cowardice, which makes the scorn sharper.

thinai_evidence.note: two sides' horses meeting at the battle-front

comparisons.tenor: the poor chief's horse cleaving the army
the rich kings' horses holding back

300.reading: You cry 'give me a shield, give me a shield', but even with a shield behind a boulder you will not escape: the younger brother of the man you killed yesterday evening, his eyes whirling like kunri seeds dropped in a lamp, is searching for you as men search the great town for the one house where toddy was brewed.
300.nuance: The revenge is a kinsman's duty, so the killing of yesterday makes today's enemy; lines 5 and 6 also compare the search to a hunt for toddy, but the phrase ஓர் இல் கோயின் is unclear and is left out of the comparisons.

thinai_evidence.note: a taunt to an enemy warrior in battle

comparisons.tenor: the avenging brother's red whirling eyes

links.note: 281 lists the rites for guarding a wounded man's life (neem in the house, mustard, kaanchi sung, incense); 296 shows the same rites (வேம்புசினை ஒடிப்பவும், காஞ்சி பாடவும், ஐயவி புகைப்பவும்) in every house while the hero's chariot is late.
links.teaches: Read together the two show the rite was done not only over a wound already seen but in anticipation, by every house in the village, so 296's anxiety is the same guarding as 281 started before the news has come.

links.note: 282: the hero's body is gone and only his split shield remains, but he is in the mouths of poets; Kural 235: a death that is really existence comes only to the skilled.
links.teaches: The Kural's paradox of a death that is life gets in 282 its working mechanism: the poets' tongues are where the vanished hero now exists, so the Kural's 'skilled' death depended on someone to sing it.

links.note: 283 line 6 names the assembly hall of the Kosar (கோசர் அவைக்களத்தானும்); Akananuru 262 names the town-elder Kosar (ஊர்முது கோசர்) who blinded Anni Mignili's father.
links.teaches: Both poets know the Kosar as a body that sits in judgment, an institution in the puram fragment and the source of a borrowed story in the akam poem, so the Kosar's council was famous enough for an akam speaker to cite it as a known wrong.

links.note: 283 names the Azhumbil man who will not submit (அழும்பிலன் அடங்கான்); Akananuru 44 uses Azhumbil (அழும்பில் அன்ன அறாஅ யாணர்) as the measure of unfailing plenty, in a Chola king's praise.
links.teaches: The akam poet uses Azhumbil only as a by-word for wealth, while the puram fragment remembers it as the seat of a man who resisted, so the same place carried prosperity in love poetry and defiance in war poetry.

links.note: 284: the warrior who killed an elephant laughs at the back of the man who fled; Kural 774: having sent his spear off with an elephant, he laughs as he pulls one from his own body.
links.teaches: Both place a warrior's laugh just after an elephant kill, but 284 turns it on the coward and the Kural turns it on the hero's own wound, which shows the Kural moving the scorn of fear from the enemy to the self.

links.note: 297 says cool fields (தண்ணடை) are the due of speared warriors; 285 shows a lord bowing his head when a warrior he had given only a barren small village (கரம்பைச் சீறூர்) dies, the fertile fields left out.
links.teaches: 297 states the warrior's claim to good land; 285 shows what happened when a lord fell short of it, the shame made public at the death, so the grant was a debt the community watched.

links.note: 286 says her son was not laid on the bier and covered in pure white cloth (தூவெள் அறுவை போர்ப்பித்திலதே); 291 has the dead hero lying under pure white cloth (தூவெள் அறுவை மாயோன்) on the field.
links.teaches: 291 shows the white cloth as the covering given to a fallen warrior, which fixes the sense of 286's last line: the mother speaks of the shroud and bier of the dead, not of illness or bed, so her son's death is in question either way.

links.note: 287 says the warriors who do not run, if they die, enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the high world; Kural 777 names only world-circling fame as what those who do not want life seek.
links.teaches: The Kural names fame alone and its commentator adds heaven; 287 already makes heaven the reward and dismisses land, so the commentator's addition had a Sangam warrant that the Kural itself left out.

links.note: 288 ends with the kites crowding the dead warrior's chest so that no one can embrace him; in 291 the mourner tells the children to keep the birds' clamour off the dead man and drives away the jackal herself.
links.teaches: Together they show the birds at the body as the thing the living had to fight, so 291's guarding is the answer to 288's loss: the kin's last duty was to take back the body from the birds.

links.note: 289: like a ploughman choosing the best bull, the king picks the man among the old fighting houses and gives him his own gold bowl; Kural 517: having reasoned that this man will do this by this means, leave it to him.
links.teaches: The Kural's choice of the right man for a task appears in 289 as a public honour, the king's own bowl handed over before battle, so the selection the Kural treats as reasoning was also a gift that bound the chosen man to go first.

links.note: 289 ends with the drum crying 'today is the taking of flowers' (பூக்கோள் இன்று); 293, whose colophon thurai is பூக்கோட் காஞ்சி, follows the war-drum's call to the flower-selling woman who must go into other houses.
links.teaches: 289 hears the flower-taking from the camp as an honour; 293 hears the same call from the village and sees the flower-seller's trade and the wives' loss, so the one ritual is shown from both ends.

links.note: 290: this man's grandfather died beside the king's grandfather, and he too will take the spears meant for the king; Kural 764: an army is one with courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்).
links.teaches: The Kural's 'courage that has come down' is, in Avvaiyar, a three-generation bond between one fighting family and one royal family, so inherited courage meant inherited loyalty to a particular house.

links.note: 290 asks the king to give this warrior toddy before he drinks himself; 298's warrior complains the king gave his men the dregs and drank the clear, and now does not send him first.
links.teaches: Together they show the order of drinking as the measure of the order of dying: 290 asks for the first cup on the strength of the family's dead, 298 reads a poor cup as the loss of the vanguard.

links.note: 292 defends a warrior who stopped the king's toddy being mixed and will not wait his turn; 298 has a warrior angry that the king does not tell him 'you go first'.
links.teaches: Both turn a quarrel over drink into a claim to the front line, which shows the feast's order was read as a promise about the battle, and a warrior who seized one was claiming the other.

links.note: 294: no one approaches the warrior standing alone, as no one approaches the gem the serpent spits (அரவுஉமிழ் மணியின் குறுகார்); Kural 763: a host of rats roaring like the sea perish when the cobra breathes.
links.teaches: The Kural's cobra verse never mentions an army and its commentator reads it as one hero against a crowd; 294 uses the serpent exactly so, for a lone fighter in a confused battle whom the crowd will not approach, so the allegorical reading follows an image of the war poems.

links.note: 295: seeing her son broken in the battle press, his mother's dry breasts flow; Kural 69: a mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him.
links.teaches: The Kural's mother hears praise and her joy exceeds the birth; Avvaiyar's mother sees the body and her breasts give milk as at the birth, so the Kural's comparison with childbirth has a harsher Sangam form in which the worth was proved by dying.

links.note: Both have the thurai உவகைக் கலுழ்ச்சி; in 278 a mother who swore to cut off the breast that fed him if he fled finds him dead facing the enemy; in 295 the mother's withered breasts flow on seeing his glory.
links.teaches: The two poems make the mother's breast the measure of the son's conduct, cut off for flight in 278 and filled again for his death in 295, so the thurai of joyful weeping has a fixed bodily sign.

links.note: 297 says it is right that cool fields (தண்ணடை) be given to speared warriors; 287 asks what getting cool fields is (தண்ணடை பெறுதல் யாவது?) to men who, if they die, enjoy the high world.
links.teaches: One poem claims the land grant as the warrior's due and the other waves it aside for heaven, so the war poems held two accounts of the hero's wage, and which one a poet used depended on whether he spoke for the living or the willing dead.

links.note: 299: the poor chief's gram-fed horse cleaves the front while the rich kings' ghee-fed horses hang back; Kural 769: an army wins if it is free of shrinking, lasting grievance and poverty (வறுமை).
links.teaches: The Kural counts poverty among the things that lose a war, while 299 makes the poor chief the winner and the rich the ones who shrink, so the Kural's rule is about an army's supply and the poem's point is that wealth does not supply courage.

new_concepts.gloss: the state of helpless grief after a patron's or lord's death, and the lament that voices it
new_concepts.label_source: label is ours here; 291 is such a lament over a dead warrior (விளரிக் கொட்பின், line 4)

new_concepts.gloss: an old house of fighting men, whose sons go to war generation after generation
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: மூதி லாளன் in 284 line 4 and மூதி லாளர் in 289 line 5; the colophon thurai of 288 is மூதின் முல்லை

source_issues: 282 line 4 is a dotted gap; the colophon has no thinai or thurai. Marked from the lines present.
283 lines 7 and 12 are gaps (line 12 is flagged for a word beginning with a dead consonant), and line 3 differs in another edition; the poem is marked uncertain.
284: the colophon thurai பண்பாட்டு looks like a misprint for பாண்பாட்டு, the thurai of 283 under the same thinai; puram_thurai name corrected.
285 lines 5 and 9 are gaps; line 12 ends தனனெ, likely a misprint for தனனே.
288 line 7 is a gap, which held who came to embrace the dead man.
289: the colophon has no thinai or thurai.

295 line 6: மாண்புகண் டருவி is கண்டு அருவி in sandhi; the karu form keeps the written டருவி. 295 line 7: வாடுமலை reads best as வாடுமுலை (withered breasts), the sense the mother's milk requires; மலை for முலை.

296: the colophon thurai எறான் முல்லை is a misspelling of ஏறாண் முல்லை; puram_thurai name corrected. The review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; it carries the neem-breaking that matches 281, so it is marked as it stands.

297: the colophon thurai இண்டாட்டு looks like a misprint for உண்டாட்டு, the vetchi thurai of the victors' toddy feast, which suits the poem's toddy (line 6); puram_thurai name corrected. The colophon has no poet.
298: the colophon's poet, thinai and thurai were filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition; another edition gives the poet as ஆலியார்.
